facts.claim: "You're Gonna Cry" was released as a single on July 21, 2022, on the DWLLRS label. It runs 3:39 and is listed as alternative.
The song was written by Bren Eissman and Joey Spurgeon, the two members of DWLLRS.
The single is copyrighted ℗ 2022 DWLLRS. Apple Music lists it as a one-song single.
DWLLRS are singer/guitarists Bren Eissman and Joey Spurgeon, who both grew up in San Clemente, California.
Their first single, "And Then We'll Be Alright," came out at the start of 2020. In 2022 they signed to Island Records and went viral with "Float Through the Ceiling" and "Blue Spirits."
The band name comes from "to dwell", a term Bren's dad coined sarcastically about the pair's tendency to overthink everything.
Bren and Joey say they grew close through late-night dorm-room conversations about existential dread and a shared tendency to overthink. Joey said, "We just tend to dwell on stuff."
Bren and Joey met at a basketball camp in sixth grade, went to the same high school, and later became college roommates. That is when they started the project.
Bren said he wants DWLLRS music to feel like driving down PCH in high school, crying and listening to Current Joys.
A review of their Voodoo Room show cites Dominic Fike and Frank Ocean as vocal influences, and Brockhampton and Roy Blair as influences on the experimental production.

research.lineage: DWLLRS sit in the lo-fi, bedroom-made indie/alt-pop scene of the California coast, with hazy, nostalgic, minimalist songs that went viral on TikTok.

draft:
The chorus of **You're Gonna Cry** pulls a strange trick. It opens with an apology, "Believe me, I'm sorry," then predicts your tears three times over, then swings out to the end of everything: "You're gonna cry, we're gonna die, we're so right." Grief, mortality, and a teenager's total certainty all land in one breath, and DWLLRS don't pick a winner. The narrator is apologizing for a hurt that hasn't happened yet, and seems almost proud to be the one who saw it coming.

That fits a duo who named themselves after a habit. Bren Eissman and Joey Spurgeon, who wrote the song together, took "DWLLRS" from "to dwell," a word Bren's dad used sarcastically about how much the two overthink. Here the dwelling runs both ways. The verses look back: old friends laughing, a failed raid on a parents' liquor cabinet, a first kiss that turned to ashes. Each one ends in a shrug that's really a verdict: "It never works, it never worked." The past tense and present tense sitting next to each other is the whole song in small. What failed then is still failing now.

The second verse admits even more. Over a plea to be held like something holy, the narrator says the quiet part: "I keep lying to myself, but I think it's working out." There's no irony in the delivery. It's a person half-watching their own self-deception and choosing to keep it going because it helps.

The sound keeps all of this gentle. A clean electric guitar rolls through arpeggiated chords with a slight delay, over a simple root-note bass line and a steady mid-tempo beat, with open hi-hats on the off-beats. The vocal is clean and a little breathy, and harmonies stack up behind certain phrases until the lines feel crowded with company. The production is polished, with a modest room reverb. That's tidier than the bedroom-pop scene of the California coast the duo came up in, but the nostalgic haze is the same. The calm groove under lyrics about inevitable heartbreak is the point. It sounds like someone explaining the worst news kindly.

Bren has said he wants their music to feel like driving down PCH in high school, crying to Current Joys, and the closing stretch shows what he means. The prediction turns inward: "I'll be crying over love." Then the lines start to repeat and break off mid-phrase, as if the overthinking has finally run out of words.

It sticks because it apologizes for your heartbreak before it happens, and by the end you can tell the singer is mostly bracing for their own.
